data.title: Chieftains, princes and kings of the Sorbian, Lusatian and Spree–Havel Slavs (Peter Šalkovský)
data.excerpt: After the fall of the Thuringian kingdom in 531, only scattered groups of Saxons and Thuringians remained east of the Elbe, and Slavs began to move into the vacated land along the Elbe, the Saale and the Havel. Peter Šalkovský follows the chieftains, princes and kings of the Sorbs, the Milceni, the Lusatians, the Havelli and the Spreveni down to the end of Slavic rule in Brandenburg in 1150.
data.metaTitle: Šalkovský: elites of the Sorbian and Lusatian Slavs

children.text: As we have already mentioned in the article on the Obodrite and Veleti elites, after the fall of the Thuringian kingdom in 531 only individual groups of Saxons or Thuringians remained in the territory east of the Elbe. Subsequently, until the end of the 6th century, the territory became in terms of power something like no man’s land, which was also reflected in the lack of interest of contemporary authors. And it was probably only at this time that Slavs from the Bohemian Elbe region could begin to move further into the vacated space along the Elbe, the Saale and the Havel as far as central Germany. The beginnings of Slavic occupation by the Prague-type culture are placed here at the end of the 6th and in the first half of the 7th century. The remainder of the eastern parts of Germany roughly as far as the Elbe, and its north – Western Pomerania up to Rügen and eastern Holstein – was occupied somewhat later and gradually, predominantly from the north-western current, by the early Slavic Sukow-Dziedzice culture, which was probably a regional northern derivative of the Prague-type culture.
In the period from the 9th to the 11th century, more than 70 tribal territories and small tribes are named in various charters and chronicles in the territories of the north-western Slavs.

children.text: In the present-day German southern Elbe region, the Saale region as far as the Oder and the Neisse, a large group of tribes were the Lusatian Sorbs in present-day Lusatia and in Saxony, bounded on the west by the Saale and separated on the north by a belt of forest. The river Elbe divided them into two larger groups composed of several smaller tribes (Fig. 1). The main reason why the Sorbian tribes never created a larger and longer-lasting principality or tribal confederation was the decentralisation of the largest tribes. No more permanent, firm power centre arose here from which a unifying process could have started. In the short term, however, tribal groupings did come into being here.

Already between the years 631–632, Fredegar mentions the prince of the united Sorbs, “dux gente Surbiorum” Dervan (Dervanus). Then a certain vacuum occurs in the sources. Only at the beginning of the 9th century were the princes Melito, “rex superbus qui regnebat in Siurbis”, and “dux” Miliduch, defeated by the armies of Charlemagne, described in a similar way. The prince of a confederation mostly came from the strongest member tribe, was entrusted with the supreme command of the confederate army and likewise represented the confederation externally, acting in its name. If the threat continued after the death of the confederate prince, a new leader was chosen by common consensus. The confederation of the Sorbs corresponded best to the definition of a tribal confederation. The report of the Bavarian Geographer provides sufficient information about this: “Iuxta illos est regio [i.e. the confederation], quae uocatur Surbo in qua regione plures [i.e. a higher tribal unit] sunt quae habent ciuitates”. The fifty civitates mentioned formed several regio under the leadership of princes, who later, at the tribal assembly, together with the leaders of the individual civitates (seniores, primores), elected the supreme confederate prince (dux, dux gente Surbiorum, rex Superbus).

The first royal stronghold of the Sorbs – Königsburg (civitas Kesigesburch), identified with the site of Cösitz – is documented in writing for the year 839. The ramparts of the Cösitz stronghold, but also of Dresden-Briesnitz or Zehren, were provided with both a front and a rear wall of dried mud bricks and stones. The width of the walls, however, used to be smaller and usually did not exceed 1 m. They tend to be connected with East Frankish influence on the local Slavic defensive architecture in the 9th–10th centuries.

In 840, in a battle with the Saxons near it, the prince of the Sorbian Colodici, Czimislav, fell. Kesigesburch was taken, and with it 11 further Sorbian fortresses between the rivers Saale and Elbe also had to submit to Saxon power, at least temporarily. The Sorbian Cösitz was one of the most massive in central Germany, it also had a large fortified bailey, it was situated in waterlogged terrain that was difficult to access, and it remained in use even by the German settlers after the territory was incorporated into the Saxon Eastern, later the Meißen, march.

The tribes east of the Elbe, between the rivers Elbe, Schwarze Elster, Bober and the Oder, are sometimes regarded as a separate group of (White) Croats, who were divided into the Milceni, the Lusatians, the Dadosesani, the Trebovyane, the Bobrzanie, the Silesians and the Croats proper.

The tribes of the Milceni (Milzane, Milcini) living in Upper Lusatia had, according to the Bavarian Geographer, 30 strongholds in the 9th century, which must also have had their own “lords”. Other, less well known tribes are mentioned here as well (Selpoli, Licicaviki, Treboviani), which evidently were not without their chieftains either. According to the records of the chronicler Thietmar, the seat of the Milceni prince Dobromir at the turn of the 10th and 11th centuries was the Ortenburg in Bautzen, but besides that there existed here above all many typical small circular fortresses (Brohna, Seelitz-Biesern), evidently with their own local magnates.

Further north, the Lusatians (Lunsici) settled in Lower Lusatia had 30 strongholds; the central one was probably Liubus, or Lubusz, provisionally located at the site of Borchelt in the cadastral area of the village of Freesdorf (Luckau). The dendrochronological dates for the small Lusatian circular lowland strongholds of the Tornow type in Lower Lusatia (Brandenburg) and Saxony-Anhalt, previously dated conventionally earlier, suggest that they came into being only at the end of the 9th and in the first decades of the 10th century. At that time, in view of the ever-growing threats from the East Frankish Empire, or the German kingdom, many such new strongholds were to be built here, evidently also as a consequence of the absence of a stronger domestic central power, or of its great fragmentation in the hands of many members of the lower tribal elites.

These small forts of the Tornow type were the seats of clan or lower tribal chieftains and at the same time served as places of refuge for the inhabitants of the open baileys. They were concentrated above all in the tribal territories of the Lusatians and the Milceni. They often measured only 30–60 m in diameter, most of which was taken up by the rampart and the casemates around its circuit, so that no larger area remained for the inner enclosure. One of several such almost completely investigated strongholds was Tornow (Fig. 2), or the stronghold at Raddusch (Vetschau) on the Spree (Fig. 3), which was already completely reconstructed in the last century, after archaeological investigation. The power of the clan chieftains in the individual stronghold districts was consolidated here and the strongholds gradually took on a character similar to that of magnates’ residences, often independent of the central power.

In 932 the German king Henry I subjugated the Milceni and the Lusatians. He attached the Milceni to the Meißen march and the Lusatians to the Eastern (from 965 the Lusatian) march, and thus severed them from the other related tribes. The local Slavic elites were removed and replaced by German ones. The territories between the Elbe and the Oder then temporarily, until 983, became part of the German state, which established new marches here and built new strongholds, the so-called Burgwarde (Meißen, Zehren, Gehren), which, however, did not differ fundamentally in their buildings or in their fortification from Slavic strongholds. Bishoprics were also founded in Brandenburg and Meißen and an archbishopric in Magdeburg, by means of which an intensive Christianisation from above was carried out.

children.text: The Lusatian-Sorbian territories now remained permanently part of the Lusatian and Meißen marches. In the east, at the beginning of the 11th century, they briefly came under Bohemian or Polish administration. From 1002 to 1031 Lusatia was in Polish hands, and from the 12th century it was again gradually settled by a German population. In the new imperial territories and their centres, the population of Slavic origin also often retained a significant position, mostly already loyal to the new state and, in the militarily harsh times of the 10th–11th centuries, having an interest in local political stability and economic prosperity. Not to mention the relations of the political and military elites, which point rather to a partnership-based and pragmatic cooperation, often founded on personal or even family ties, than to national or religious prejudice and rejection.

Further north, separated from them by a belt of primeval forest and flooded land between the middle Elbe and the basins of the Havel and the Spree, lived the Havelli (Stodorani), the Spreveni, the Dossani and the Plonians. Among their oldest strongholds were Brandenburg and Berlin-Spandau (Fig. 4).

children.text: The leading position among them was held by the Havelli, with eight strongholds and an island centre at Brandenburg on the Havel (Brena, Brennaburg, 929). It had a key strategic position, recorded by chroniclers, according to whom from the 9th to the middle of the 12th century alone, that is, during roughly 330 years of its existence, in the course of the fighting between the Slavs, the Germans and the Poles, it changed its owners as many as 13 times. In 928, during the first German expansion, it was taken thanks to the frozen Havel and its prince Tugomir was captured. Both the Havelli and the Spreveni became subjects of the German king Henry I, and the eastern territories between the Elbe and the Oder became part of the northern Billung and the southern Saxon march.

In 983, however, the Havelli too joined the uprising of the Slavic tribes and for the following 150 years freed themselves from German rule. The strongholds were taken again and only the territories west of the Elbe remained in German hands. The central German Slavic tribes, however, remained politically fragmented, and therefore in the following century they became the target of military raids and devastation from both the German and the Polish side. Only under the rule of the last Brandenburg prince Pribislav, after 1127, did the situation stabilise, evidently through the rendering of homage to the German king. The territory of the Havelli principality then expanded from Brandenburg to Spandau. The rule of Slavic princes in the Havelli principality ends with the death of Prince Pribislav in 1150. From 1157, after several years of fighting, Brandenburg came definitively under German administration and became the centre of the new March of Brandenburg.

children.text: The main stronghold of the Spreveni tribe was Copnic, similar to the Spandau stronghold (Fig. 4), lying on an island at Berlin-Köpenick at the confluence of the river Dahme with the Spree. At this stronghold the Spreveni prince Jaczo (Jaxa), at that time a vassal of the Polish king, even struck his own coins around 1150 (Fig. 5). The respect for history and for important personalities (not only of German origin) within the German nation is also attested by a memorial, and not an isolated one – the column of Prince Jaczo in the Grunewald (Berlin-Charlottenburg), erected on the orders of the Prussian king Friedrich Wilhelm IV as early as 1845 (and renewed a hundred years later), and the cultural and recreational festival (Jaczo-Fest), which has been held here in his name since 2011 on the Schildhorn peninsula in the river Havel (Fig. 6).

The permanent German colonisation of these territories, which began in the western areas between the Saale and the Elbe in the 9th century and ended in the Havel region as far as the left bank of the Oder, that is, in the territories of present-day Saxony and Brandenburg, in the middle of the 12th century, brought with it not only a new population but also a new territorial-administrative organisation, that of the so-called stronghold wardenships – Burgwarde – that is, territories administered by a warden acting as the plenipotentiary of the German prince or king in a centre with a stronghold.

blocks.alt: Fig. 5. A coin – a bracteate of Prince Jaczo from Köpenick.

children.text: Of the original Slavs, only a few tens of thousands of Lusatian Sorbs have survived here to this day, culturally and linguistically, in Saxony and Brandenburg, in the basin of the upper course of the Spree, in parts of the territory of old Upper and Lower Lusatia, in the position of a national minority. According to official information from extrapolations from the 1990s, about 60,000 of them live here. On the basis of self-identification, 45,000 to 50,000 were recorded, and on the basis of active knowledge of the language, around 67,000 Lusatian Sorbs. At present most of them also speak German. They speak Upper Sorbian, which is close to medieval Czech, and Lower Sorbian, which is closer to Polish. They live mainly in the Saxon districts of Bautzen (Budyšín), Niesky, Kamenz and Bischofswerda, and in Brandenburg in the districts of Hoyerswerda, Weißwasser and Senftenberg, and above all in Cottbus (Chotebuz) and its surroundings. Sorbian is taught in primary and secondary schools as a first, second or foreign language. In Brandenburg and Saxony there are television (ORB, Ostdeutscher Rundfunk Brandenburg) and radio broadcasts in this language, even if only for a few hours. Sorbian is also taught in courses in Bautzen and Cottbus. Teachers of Lusatian Sorbian study at the Institute of Sorbian Studies of the University of Leipzig.

children.text: The Lusatian Sorbs also have their own organisation – the Domowina, the Sorbian Institute within the German Academy of Sciences, the Sorbian Museum in Bautzen and several local cultural and social organisations and foundations.
PhDr. Peter Šalkovský, DrSc., Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences.
